visible.summary:
A trans visitor in Manisa is subject to the same nationwide developments as anywhere else in the country. An October 2025 leaked omnibus draft would amend the penal code to imprison acts deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality (up to three years; up to four for same-sex ceremonies), restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people 25 and over under infertility and repeated-evaluation conditions, and expose doctors to up to seven years in prison; national monitoring reports that 2025 hostility became explicit state policy — family-year directives from the head of state, a rights organisation closed, broadcast and arts-event censorship, three hate-motivated killings, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations and a 2.5-fold rise in detentions.

No statute, incident or court case specific to Manisa appears in the surviving sources for this record: the documents behind it are national-level and carry no provincial breakdown. The absence of province-specific documentation is not evidence of local tolerance — the nationwide framework and its 2025-26 escalation reach this province as any other.
visible.tangentialFactors: Draft same-sex-conduct criminalisation (the leaked 11th Judicial Package, Oct 2025: up to 3-4 years) and 2025's institutionalised hostility (six right-to-life violations, 313 liberty violations, one LGBTI+ organisation closed) are national-LGB-and-trans factors that shape police and official posture toward gender-nonconforming people in this province as well; public-activity bans by governors in peer provinces signal the same climate.
visible.localsOnly: The civil code's 'Changing Sex' provisions — gender-marker procedure, and the leaked draft's proposed care-age rise to 25 with mandatory infertility and government-approved hospital evaluation — plus the Health Ministry's trans-healthcare regulations bear on residents rather than visitors.

National-level document; no province-specific content for this unit.

Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Manisa included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised; marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed the registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from the military, and since 2015 authorities have banned pride events in most years, using tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions against those who defied the bans; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49. The page records a February 2026 press report of legislation considering criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison, which was not included in the 2026 omnibus (the 12th judicial package), and September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involving 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26): in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In June 2025 the health ministry's medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, despite existing law permitting access from 18. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association for sharing 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - criminalising expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and making legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

visible.summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for this province. That absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not local permissiveness: the nationwide framework applies in full.

As documented nationally: an October 2025 draft judicial package would criminalise conduct judged contrary to biological sex or general morality (up to three years) and same-sex ceremonies (up to four), bar gender-affirming care below 25 behind an infertility assessment, and expose patients and providers to prosecution — protested by civic groups and the medical association. The national LGBTI monitor's 2025 report describes hostility as explicit state policy: 'family' directives to institutions, a first organisational closure in years, 3 hate-motivated killings, 89 ill-treatment violations, 299 detention decisions. July 2025 saw mass identity-check roundups in which police detained trans women and recorded names and images without stated grounds.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Kurdish-majority south-east runs on heightened security practice (state-of-emergency legacies, village-guard system, high police presence), producing more routine identity checks than the national average — amplifying the exposure of any gender-nonconforming traveller stopped for identity verification.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): HRW, 29 Oct 2025, reports a leaked omnibus reform draft ("11th Judicial Package") that would amend the Turkish penal code to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison and participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four; it would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, mandate permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and expose both healthcare professionals performing such care and patients to criminal prosecution, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; HRW calls for its withdrawal.

National-framework monitoring report (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): Kaos GL's Human Rights Report 2025, titled "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy, with instructions issued to public institutions under the "Year of the Family" banner. It documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected, 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (a striking increase over the prior year), 313 right-to-liberty violations - about 2.5 times the previous year - with 299 detention decisions, freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540, and 40 right-to-association violations including the first closure of an LGBTI+ association in many years.
